findings.body: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.`, producing an unhandled 500 error instead of paginated results; the comment's claim that the ORM handles negative slicing is false.
findings.evidence: start_offset = cursor.offset  # Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination
findings.failure_mode: Runtime AssertionError/500 on attacker-controllable cursor input.
findings.impact: `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.`, producing an unhandled 500 error instead of paginated results; the comment's claim that the ORM handles negative slicing is false.
findings.root_cause: New advanced-features branch deliberately feeds an unvalidated negative cursor offset into a Django queryset slice, which Django prohibits.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not pass negative offsets to Django slicing; clamp with `max(0, cursor.offset)` or reject negative offsets with a BadPaginationError before slicing.
findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative offset crashes on Django slice
findings.trigger: An admin / global-access member calls the audit-log endpoint with `?optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor whose offset component is negative (e.g. `cursor=<value>:-5:0`), so `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch lines R877-R882 show that when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code passes `start_offset = cursor.offset` (negative) directly to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django querysets raise AssertionError on negative slice indices. The comment on R876 falsely claims Django handles negative slicing. Trigger is realistic: admin with `optimized_pagination=true` and negative cursor offset.

raw_findings.body: Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects are no longer joined correctly (previously supported up to 10000), and the explanatory comment documenting this exact limitation was deleted, so the regression is undocumented.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Deep segment trees join incorrectly with no code documentation of the limit.
raw_findings.impact: Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects are no longer joined correctly (previously supported up to 10000), and the explanatory comment documenting this exact limitation was deleted, so the regression is undocumented.

raw_findings.body: Segments are truncated at a hardcoded 1000 spans regardless of the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config, and eviction happens silently with no metric, so operators cannot tune the cap or observe dropped spans.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Config divergence and silent data loss during span eviction.
raw_findings.impact: Segments are truncated at a hardcoded 1000 spans regardless of the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config, and eviction happens silently with no metric, so operators cannot tune the cap or observe dropped spans.
raw_findings.root_cause: Cap value duplicated as a magic number in Lua instead of being driven by the existing configuration.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Pass the configured max span count into the script as an ARGV parameter and emit a metric when `zpopmin` evicts spans.
raw_findings.title: Eviction threshold hardcoded to 1000, ignoring configurable max_segment_spans
raw_findings.trigger: SpansBuffer is constructed with a non-default `max_segment_spans` (default is 1001), while the Lua script always caps at the literal 1000.

raw_findings.body: The `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric/log is no longer emitted and `self.max_segment_spans` (still set to 1001) becomes dead configuration, removing observability that this eviction change was supposed to preserve.

raw_findings.root_cause: The only consumer of `max_segment_spans` was deleted without removing or repurposing the config.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Either drive eviction/observability from `max_segment_spans` or remove the now-unused config field to avoid dead code.
